Chapter 6. Listening to Understand—the Heart of Empathic Communication.
When you’ve built trust and embraced a win-win mindset, the next step is to master empathic communication. So, what does that really mean? It’s all about making the choice to seek first to understand before trying to be understood.
Imagine this: instead of waiting for your turn to talk, or thinking about your next point, you’re focused on truly getting where the other person is coming from. You’re listening—not just with your ears, but with your heart.
Picture empathic listening like tuning in to someone else’s frequency. You’re not filtering their words through your own assumptions, and you’re not rushing in with advice. Instead, you’re stepping into their world for a moment—seeing things through their eyes, and feeling what they feel.
It goes deeper than just the words you hear. You’re picking up on their tone, their body language, and even the emotions simmering just beneath the surface.
Here’s a simple way to think about it: like being a mirror. When someone feels truly seen and heard, it’s as if you’re reflecting their experience back to them. That feeling of validation builds trust. And it’s especially powerful during conflict or when there’s a misunderstanding—those moments when our natural reaction might be to defend ourselves or persuade the other person.
But if you pause, and really listen, you can help dial down the tension and actually open the door to real connection.
So, how do you actually practice empathic listening? Here are a few simple ways:
First, try reflecting back what you’ve heard. That means paraphrasing what the other person just said, to check that you’ve really understood.
Next, ask clarifying questions. Gently probe for more detail or context—without any judgment.
And maybe the toughest one: resist the urge to jump in and fix things. Sometimes, the best thing you can do is just hold space for what the other person is feeling, instead of rushing in with solutions.
Think about a parent listening to a frustrated teenager. Instead of brushing off those feelings or immediately offering advice, the parent might say, “It sounds like you’re really overwhelmed by your workload right now.” That simple reflection can make the teenager feel seen and understood, which makes it a lot easier to work together toward solutions.
Once you’ve established real understanding, then it’s your turn—to share your own perspective, clearly and respectfully.
This two-way process—first understanding, then being understood—that’s what builds a strong foundation for solving problems and working together. It shifts conversations from a tug-of-war of opinions to a chance for shared meaning.
Sure, empathic communication isn’t always easy—especially when emotions are running high, or the stakes feel big. It takes patience, humility, and the willingness to set aside your own agenda for a little while.
But over time, this habit deepens relationships and creates a space where creativity and real cooperation can thrive.
